01

The Basics & Key Concepts

Adverts are analysed for media language, representation and contexts. Before the set texts, four concepts you must be able to use.

The concept the exam loves: polysemy

  • Media language — how meaning is constructed through VATLs (Visual, Audio, Technical codes and Language/Mode of Address).
  • Denotation — what a sign literally is. Connotation — the meanings it suggests.
  • Polysemic — signs and symbols are open to many interpretations. The meaning depends on how the signs are "read" — and on the cultural background of the reader.
  • Anchorage — the words that accompany an image fix ("anchor") its meaning. Change the caption and you change the meaning; an open text becomes a closed one.
Anchorage in action: the text anchors the meaning of the main image. "What a delicious dilemma!" — what TWO meanings does this have?

What the exam wordings mean

  • Images = visual codes — costume, posture, expression, hair, make-up…
  • Text/written language = what the words say about audience; connotations, techniques.
  • Layout and design = where assets are placed and why; font size and colour.

02

Quality Street — Media Language

Mackintosh's Quality Street, 1956. "What a delicious dilemma! 18 delightfully different toffees and chocolates." Learn the advert inch by inch.

The set text — this is the clean copy you'll see in the exam
1956
Year of the advert
1936
Quality Street launched by Mackintosh's — a chocolate box affordable to everyone, not just the wealthy
18
"Delightfully different" toffees and chocolates
Post-war
Rationing ends; by the mid-50s working people could afford small luxuries again

Historical context — why it matters

  • The 1956 advert came as Britain emerged from post-WWII rationing, when food and clothing were limited and controlled by the government.
  • Chocolate was still a rare treat — a luxury for special occasions like Christmas and birthdays, not an everyday item.
  • The Conservative Party's 1951 election campaign slogan — "Set the People Free" — captured the mood: drastic changes in entertainment and consumption as goods became more affordable.

The Regency era & intertextuality

The picture-frame characters are Miss Sweetly and Major Quality — part of the brand identity since 1936. They are symbolic of the Regency era (the age of the Prince Regent, George IV, 1811–1837), associated with elegance in architecture, furniture and design.

This is intertextuality — one text referencing another. Borrowing Regency imagery connotes quality, tradition, refinement and Britishness — exactly what the brand name promises.

The Regency era: elegance and refinement
Miss Sweetly & Major Quality — brand icons since 1936

The three exam areas, mapped onto the advert

AreaKey analysis points
Text / written languageAlliteration: "delicious dilemma", "delightfully different" — playful, memorable, polysemic (the dilemma = choosing between 18 sweets… or the man choosing between the two women, or the women choosing the sweets/the man). Superlatives express high quality. The elegant script font of the logo connotes tradition, sophistication and an educated audience. The text anchors the image.
Layout & designThe ornate gold frame connotes opulence and wealth — and acts like a halo around the man. The main figures form a shape that leads the eye down to the product at the centre-bottom. Font sizes create hierarchy: brand name largest. The women are dressed in the colours of the sweet wrappers, visually tying them to the product.
Images / visual codesThe man's pinstripe suit, collar and tie connote success and education; his central position and relaxed expression signal status. The women's revealing dress and informality contrast with the formal males in the frame. Product close-ups (Chocolate Strawberry Cup, Harrogate Toffee, Toffee Finger) with descriptions act as the pack shot.
Two women compete for the man — or for the sweets?
All hands lead to the tin: product prominence
The pack shot: named varieties with tempting descriptions

03

Quality Street — Representation

How are gender, class and age represented — and whose view of the world does the advert construct? Remember: representation = the ways the media re-present the world.

A patriarchal narrative

The advert follows a patriarchal narrative: the man sits at the centre, relaxed and in control, holding the tin — the object of desire — while two women drape themselves over him, kissing his cheeks and reaching for the sweets. Power sits with the man; the women compete.

The link between women, the desire for chocolate, and the way women might be manipulated by men was common in 1950s advertising — as if offering the "right" chocolates was the way to a woman's affection.

In its 1956 context this fits dominant ideology: a woman's place was largely domestic, and adverts routinely showed women as decorative, emotional and defined by men. Ask: would this advert be acceptable today?

The annotated set text — your revision map (edusitesmedia)

Laura Mulvey — The Male Gaze

Mulvey argued the audience is positioned through the camera as a heterosexual male, so women are looked upon as objects. The camera lingers on the female body, and events involving women are framed by men's reactions to them.

Applied to Quality Street: the women are styled for display — dressed in the colours of the sweet wrappers, they are positioned as consumable, like the sweets themselves. Formal, uniformed men in the frame vs sexualised, informal women reinforces the gendered power divide.

Compare the 1950s wider pattern: adverts like the 1953 ALCOA bottle-cap ad ("You mean a woman can open it?") openly presented women as domestic and incapable.

Laura Mulvey — Male Gaze theory
1953: "You mean a woman can open it?"
More 1950s adverts — the norm Quality Street sat within

Class & age

  • Class: the Regency frame, the pinstripe suit and the very word "Quality" borrow upper-class imagery — yet the product was launched (1936) to be affordable to everyone. The advert sells working- and middle-class buyers a taste of aspiration.
  • Age: compare the 1936 and 1956 adverts — different ages represented, different targets. Apply Uses & Gratifications: who gets what pleasure from each?
  • Stereotypes to name in the exam: the successful suited male; the decorative, affectionate female; romance as transaction (chocolates for kisses).

Sort it: Conform or Challenge? (1950s gender stereotypes)

The man sits central, relaxed and in control, holding the object everyone wants
The women are decorative, affectionate and compete for the man's attention
Women are dressed to mirror the product — positioned as consumable, for the male gaze
The formal, uniformed men in the frame signal status and authority
The women act on their desires — they reach for the sweets and take what they want

Notice the pattern — this advert overwhelmingly conforms. That's your argument in a representation question: it reflects, rather than challenges, 1950s dominant ideology.

04

NHS 111 — "Help Us Help You" (2023)

Quality Street's companion set text — every Component 1 Section A form comes as a pair. This one is a public health campaign with no commercial aspect at all: the perfect contrast to a 1956 chocolate advert.

Commercial vs Non-commercial advertising

Commercial advertising — promotes consumer goods or services to make a profit. It persuades audiences to purchase, and usually communicates messages about a brand. (Quality Street.)

Non-commercial advertising — educates consumers or promotes ideas rather than making profit: public service announcements, charity and safety campaigns, recruitment, political ads. (NHS 111.)

What is NHS 111? A free, 24/7 service giving medical advice and urgent healthcare for non-life-threatening situations — call 111, go online, or use the NHS App. The NHS is England's publicly funded healthcare system: everyone in the UK can use it without paying full price.

Safety campaign
Public message
Recruitment
Three more non-commercial adverts — none is selling you a product
Dec 2022
Campaign launched for NHS England
M&C Saatchi
London agency; distributed by the Dept of Health & Social Care
All adults
Primary target — with extra investment in under-35s and parents of 5–12s
£0 profit
Funded by NHS England + HM Government — purely public health

Media language — the advert, piece by piece

  • Dominant image: a long shot of a father on his sick daughter's bed, set inside a UTC. No famous models — ordinary adults can identify with the scenario.
  • Costume & props: his slippers, neutral grey top and jeans; her stripy pyjamas and fairy lights — familiarity and connection.
  • Expression & gesture: his concerned face and reassuring arm convey protective care; her neutral expression and position in bed suggest sickness and dependence.
  • Propp: the father is the hero on a quest to find help; the NHS (the 111 service on his tablet) is the helper.
  • Setting: the UTC background — reception desk, leaflet rack, wipe-clean seating, clock, signage — connotes a clinical, professional, trustworthy space, and makes the colourful bed brighter by contrast.
  • Tagline: "Get to the help you need" — the imperative "get" + direct address "you" = public-health call to action.
  • Typography & colour: clear sans-serif font; simple, concise copy accessible to all literacy levels; consistent NHS blue (Pantone 300) ties everything to the brand; a muted, soft palette evokes trust and calm.
  • The warning triangle (bottom right) borrows highway warning iconography — urgency, attention.
  • Logos: HM Government (top left) + NHS (top right) = not commercial; raising awareness of a public service.
The set text — clean copy, as you'll see it in the exam. Split design: image dominates the left, concise guidance on the right; big visual grabs attention, smaller text explains how to act.

Spot the detail — the advert up close

Every crop below is a point you can make in the exam. Match the picture to the point — if you can picture the detail, you can write the paragraph.

The tagline"Get to the help you need" — imperative "get" + direct address "you". Bright white text stands out, anchoring the family to the "help" behind them.
The fatherSerious, concerned expression + direct eye contact with the camera invites trust. Protective arm reassures her; the tablet shows he's used 111 to get help.
The daughterIn bed = classic iconography of a sick child. Pink bedding, plaited pigtails and fairy lights construct her young age; she looks to her dad for care.
The slippersAnchor that he is at home — while the background says "hospital". The bed in the UTC is incongruous on purpose: 111 bridges home and urgent care.
The backgroundStaff in masks behind screens — professional, trustworthy, post-Covid. The carpet floor makes the NHS feel comfortable and welcoming.
The sign"Urgent Treatment Centre" — a prop that tells us exactly which NHS service 111 connects you to.
"Use 111"Clear instruction highlighted in NHS blue. The body copy is short, clear and jargon-free — accessible to all literacy levels. Sans-serif = modern, clear.
The NHS logoNHS blue (Pantone 300) — instant brand recognition and public trust. Paired with the HM Government logo top-left: this is a public service, not a sale.
The triangleBorrows highway warning-sign iconography — urgency, attention. "Help us help you" appeals to cooperation and community.

Representation

  • Gender: stereotypically men aren't shown as emotionally nurturing — this campaign challenges that, showing a father as primary caregiver and decision-maker in his daughter's healthcare. It reflects real change: fathers' involvement has grown from under 15 minutes a day (mid-1970s) to around 3 hours a day.
  • Ethnicity: the choice to represent a Black family is significant — Black men have been historically underrepresented in health campaigns, and groups left out of health messaging may not feel it's directed at them.
  • Age & gender of the child: constructed through plaited pigtails, pink bedding and her dependent look toward her dad.
  • Disability: the child wears a hearing aid — reflecting growing representation of the deaf community; the campaign also produced BSL versions.
  • Post-Covid context: background staff wear face masks behind plastic screens — social distancing in health settings.
  • Ethnicity — deeper points: he's in typical "dad clothes" (slippers, jeans) and presented as caring — challenging the media stereotype of the aggressive Black male. The family is normalised: no stereotyping, simply a family — communicating that NHS services are for people of all backgrounds.
  • Critical/negotiated reading: the staff in the background appear white — you could argue this implies only white people are shown as the trusted medical professionals. Staff are male and female, though, showing caregiving is not a female-only sector.

Version of reality & contexts

  • The advert constructs verisimilitude twice — the UTC and the child's bedroom are each realistic — but we're not meant to believe the bed is literally in the UTC. The combination represents how the tablet connects home to urgent care.
  • The text "Get to the help you need" framed around the model's head openly shows the advert's constructed nature — while pushing the audience to act.
  • Why the campaign exists: to ease the burden on 999 and A&E, and — post-Covid — to get the public contacting 111 first so patients get the right care safely.
  • Technology: designed for posters AND digital display, social media and search; the tablet in the image mirrors the digital service ("go online or use the NHS App") and targets under-35s and parents.

Exam practice — "Explore how the NHS 111 print advert uses media language to communicate meaning: visual codes [10]"

Starters: "The father has a … expression, which connotes… This is further anchored by…" / "The device in his hand demonstrates how he can…" / "The people in the background are wearing… this connotes…"

The father has a worried expression, which connotes he is concerned about his child. This is further anchored by his protective arm resting on her, constructing him as a caring, responsible parent. The device in his hand demonstrates how he has accessed NHS 111 for help, positioning technology as the bridge between home and urgent care. The people in the background are wearing face masks behind plastic screens, which connotes a professional, post-Covid clinical environment — reinforcing that the NHS is trustworthy and safe.
05

Exam-Style Practice

Component 1 Section A. For adverts, the most likely media language question areas are images [5], text/written language [5] and layout & design [5] — or a combination out of 15. Representation comes as the comparison with an unseen text.

Q1 · "Explore how the Quality Street advert uses media language to create meanings: (a) text/written language [5]"

Only 5 marks — get straight into your first point, don't waffle, and use PEE.

Persuasive techniques such as the polysemic alliteration "delightfully different" engage the audience. This suggests the enormous variety in the tin — but the "delicious dilemma" could also refer to the man having to choose between the two women, or the women choosing between the man and the sweets. Furthermore, the superlative "delicious" elevates the product's quality, while the elegant script font of the brand name connotes tradition and sophistication, targeting an audience that aspires to "quality".

Q2 · "Compare the representation of gender in Quality Street and the unseen advert [25]"

You must consider: the producers' choices about how to represent gender · how far the representations are similar · how far they are different. Extended response — judgements, conclusions, intro and conclusion. Spend ~10 minutes studying the unseen text first, and annotate it.

Intro: both adverts construct gender to serve their purpose — name the eras and purposes.

Similarities: women defined in relation to men; built for the male gaze (Mulvey); reflect the dominant ideology of their era.

Differences: how the unseen text's women compare to QS's active, glamorous pursuers; who holds power in the frame; how the product is anchored to gender roles.

Challenge marks: link ideologies to social and cultural context — post-war consumerism, 1950s patriarchy, and (if comparing NHS 111) modern expectations of fatherhood and inclusion.

Conclusion: a judgement on how far the representations differ and why.

Q3 · Past media language questions to practise

  • This Girl Can (2022): text/written language [5] + visual codes — images, lighting, dress [10]

"Sweating like a pig, feeling like a fox" — This Girl Can was the 2022 question text. The exam recycles the same three analysis areas across adverts, posters and front pages: master the method and any text is answerable.
